description:
Urbanova is an Engineering and Environmental Decision Support Platform connecting engineering drawings with environmental analysis, simulation, and scenario comparison.

Core Workflow: Analyze → Design → Simulate → Compare → Decide → Visualize
summary:
NASA has watched every place on Earth for more than 40 years. URBANOVA Trend Detective lets anyone, from a high-school student to a city planner, ask that record one question: "Is it changing here, how fast, and is it real or just chance?"

A student picks any place and answers two guided questions; the detective chooses from 12 NASA POWER variables (heat, rain, humidity, soil moisture, sunshine, wind), plots 45 years of monthly data and tests the trend. A planner goes further: inside URBANOVA, our urban-heat platform, every project gets its own Trend Detective that reads 40 years of Landsat images inside the site boundary.

Every answer gives a rate per decade with a 95% range, two statistical tests corrected for year-to-year memory, and a plain-language verdict, including the honest answer "not significant yet".
details:
A building designed today will stand for 50 years, but the people who plan it rarely see how the land under it has changed. NASA has the record; reading it still needs a scientist. URBANOVA Trend Detective turns that record into a tested answer in under a minute, for a student's curiosity or a planner's next project.

WHAT EXACTLY DOES IT DO?
It answers three questions about any place: Is it changing? How fast? Is the change real or just chance? It works at three scales:
1. Anywhere on Earth (public page, no account): for students and curious people. NASA POWER monthly data since 1981, 12 variables.
2. The region around a project: every URBANOVA site analysis includes the long-term climate trends of its area.
3. The plot itself: each project's Trend Detective tab reads every clear summer Landsat 5/7/8/9 image since 1984 inside the site boundary (30 m) and in the ring around it: is this plot heating up faster than its surroundings? Is it losing its green cover?

HOW DOES IT WORK?
1. Choose: two guided questions ("What are you curious about?" and "What kind of place is it?") suggest the most telling variables.
2. Fetch: live NASA POWER data (built from MERRA-2, CERES, GEWEX SRB and GPCP) and Landsat Collection 2.
3. Plot: monthly values with the seasons removed, yearly averages, and the trend line with its 95% band.
4. Measure: Sen's slope per decade with a 95% range.
5. Test: the Mann-Kendall test (Yue & Wang 2004) and a least-squares t-test with an effective sample size (Santer et al. 2000), both corrected for year-to-year memory. The verdict says "significant" only when both agree (p < 0.05).
6. Explore: "Where is it changing?" maps about 80 NASA cells around the place; a seasons chart shows which months change most; up to three places can be compared side by side; a step-change test finds the year a plot was built; results download as CSV and share as a link; an AI assistant answers questions about the results.

WHAT DID WE DISCOVER?
- New Cairo, Egypt: daytime highs +0.33 °C per decade (about +1.5 °C since 1981), significant.
- Svalbard, Arctic: +0.79 °C per decade, more than twice Cairo's rate.
- Same planet, opposite rain: the Sahel is getting wetter while south-west Australia dries; both significant.
- Delhi, India: sunshine at the ground falling (-0.61 MJ/m²/day per decade): air-pollution dimming.
- A New Cairo plot became 3.9 °C cooler than the desert around it in one step around 2005, when it was built and irrigated.
- A cleared Amazon plot (Novo Progresso, Brazil) heated +3.47 °C per decade and lost its green cover.
- Sydney rainfall: "not significant yet". The detective says so instead of drawing a misleading line.

HOW DO WE KNOW IT'S RIGHT?
- The maths: every statistic matches independent software (pymannkendall and SciPy) on 200 test series, with a largest difference of 0.
- No false alarms: on 2,000 simulated trend-free records, simple tests cried "significant" up to 28% of the time; our verdict stays at 3–6%.
- A second dataset: we repeated the analysis on Europe's ERA5 at 15 places on every continent. Temperature trends agree in direction at 100% of places; rainfall agrees at only 53%, so every rainfall result carries a warning.
- Published science: each demo agrees in direction with peer-reviewed studies (Svalbard warming, Indian solar dimming, south-west Australian drying, Sahel rain recovery).
- 396 automated tests for the science engine and 1,116 for the backend.

WHAT BENEFITS DOES IT HAVE?
- Students: learn the real workflow of a climate scientist on real NASA data: choose a variable, plot it, measure it, test it.
- Urban planners and developers: see how their exact plot and its region have changed before designing buildings that will last 50+ years.
- Cities and governments: spot plots that are heating up or losing green cover.
- Researchers: transparent, reproducible numbers with every method, source and limit stated next to the result.

HOW IS IT CREATIVE?
It is an investigation, not just a chart: guided questions, watchable demos, side-by-side places, maps of where change happens, and a detector that tells a sudden step (a plot being built) from a slow trend. It joins two scales in one tool: the whole planet for students, and one plot of land for planners.

WHAT TOOLS DID WE USE?
- Science engine: Python 3.11 (FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy, rasterio, Shapely, pyproj, Matplotlib, ReportLab), pytest.
- Backend: ASP.NET Core 10 with SQL Server (accounts, companies, projects).
- Website: React + Vite; Leaflet maps.
- Hosting: Vercel (website) and AWS EC2 (science engine and Trend Detective).
- The help assistant uses a free open AI model (gpt-oss) through Groq. An AI coding assistant (Claude, Anthropic) helped write code and documentation.

WHAT FACTORS DID WE CONSIDER?
- False alarms: climate data has year-to-year memory, so plain tests over-report trends.
- Datasets disagree, especially on rainfall.
- Satellites change instruments (Landsat changed thermal sensors in 2013), so we test both sides of each change.
- Scale: NASA POWER describes about 55 km regions; Landsat sees 30 m but only on clear summer passes.
- Free data services have limits, so the app saves what it reads and says when to try again.
- Honesty: a trend describes the past and is not a forecast. The app says so.

PROBLEMS WE FACED
- Our first tests called 28% of random records "significant". We tested several corrections by simulation and kept the one that stays near 5%.
- Building a plot changes it in one jump, which a trend test misses, so we added a step-change test.
- The Landsat archive is large and sometimes slow; a first site run takes 3–4 minutes, so the app caches every scene it reads.

WHAT WE HOPE TO ACHIEVE NEXT
More NASA instruments through Earthdata (GPM rainfall, MODIS heat and vegetation, GLDAS soil moisture), ground-station checks (NOAA GHCN), ECOSTRESS for heat at different times of day, Arabic and other languages, and a classroom mode where a teacher shares an investigation with a class.
